implementation_notes: Swift's async/await is the compiler-generated stackless coroutine: an async function's body becomes a state machine, and Task { } creates a top-level coroutine that the global concurrent executor runs on a cooperative thread pool. Structured concurrency is the organising discipline: async let and withTaskGroup bound children's lifetimes to the parent, and a child's failure or cancellation cancels the group. The critical pitfall is that an actor is NOT a coroutine and does not make its code non-blocking: an actor method that awaits between two mutations releases the actor's isolation at the await point, so another message can interleave - the same function-colouring hazard in a different form. Task priority and Task.detached (which escapes the scope) are the other decisions. The stackless form is the standard, and there is no stackful coroutine in the standard library (withTaskGroup is built on the same state machines).
idiom_name: async/await (compiler state machine) with async let and withTaskGroup for structured concurrency; Task { } to launch
pitfalls: An actor method that awaits between two mutations releases the actor's isolation at the await point, so another message can interleave - await does not hold the actor.
Task { } is unstructured: it outlives the function that created it and is not cancelled with it; use async let / withTaskGroup for structured lifetimes.
DispatchSemaphore.wait() inside an async function blocks a cooperative thread-pool thread and can deadlock the pool - use async continuations instead.
A TaskGroup child that is never awaited (or is abandoned) leaks the child's work; the group awaits all children on exit, so add them and await.
Cancellation at a suspension point throws CancellationError; a broad catch that swallows it leaves the task running and breaks structured cancellation.
